title: Young Muslims
hook: youth groups, nasheed, online study circles

segments.voice: Yesterday, hijab: in the Qur'an a curtain, today a head-covering worn in different styles for reasons women give themselves. Your line: a choice of devotion. Whose story did you ask for instead of telling? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

A Thursday night video call. Small squares on a screen: a student in a dorm room with headphones on, a young nurse just off shift, someone in a parked car with the dome light on. One of them shares a page of tafsir, a commentary on the Qur'an, and they read it together, line by line, and argue gently about what it means. Somebody's little brother wanders into frame and waves. Nobody planned this in a mosque office. They planned it in a group chat. This is one picture of young Muslims, and the Qur'an has its own pictures of the young, starting in a cave.
screen: `SQUARES ON A SCREEN.` → `A PAGE OF TAFSIR, LINE BY LINE.` → `PLANNED IN A GROUP CHAT.`

segments.voice: First, the young in the text. Surah al-Kahf tells of the people of the cave, and says of them, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance." Young people, holding on in a city that didn't share their faith. Elsewhere the Qur'an has Ibrahim's people describe him as a youth, the young man who spoke against their idols. Second, a promise kept in al-Bukhari. Among those the Prophet says Allah will shade on a day when there is no other shade, he names, in paraphrase, a young person who grew up in the worship of Allah. Growing up faithful is named on its own, in the same list as the just ruler. Third, what it looks like now. Mosque youth groups and campus student associations run study circles, sports nights, food drives and late Ramadan iftars. Nasheed, songs of praise and devotion, are sung by young voices, some with only voice and drum, because some scholars discourage instruments, and some with instruments, because others permit them. Online study circles gather young people from different cities around a text. Fourth, the hard part, said plainly. Some young Muslims carry questions about identity, about belonging, about the distance between their parents' customs and their own lives. They also carry the faith forward into new languages and new places. The people of the cave didn't wait to be old enough to matter, and neither does the Thursday night call.
screen: `THE CAVE: YOUNG MEN WHO BELIEVED.` · `SHADE FOR ONE WHO GREW UP FAITHFUL.` · `CIRCLES, NASHEED, GROUP CHATS.` · `QUESTIONS, AND CARRYING IT FORWARD.`

segments.voice: The practice: encourage a young person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger than you whose life you touch: a child, a niece, a student, a new coworker, a teenager down the street. See their face. Think of one thing they are trying to do: learn, build, believe, belong. For a few breaths, simply wish them well in it. If you pray, you can ask Allah to increase them in guidance, in your own words. Then choose one sentence of encouragement you could say to them, short and specific, and keep it ready. The bell holds the time.
Young Muslims. From the young men of the cave to youth groups, nasheed and online study circles, the young who carry the faith into new places. Today's word.

Your line: the young carry it. This week: Sufi orders today, Shia communities, the Isma'ilis, converts and reverts, Muslim women's voices, hijab, and young Muslims. Today, say your sentence of encouragement to that young person. Tomorrow, Muslims as minorities. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.
